title: FDA-Cleared AI Tool Detects Hidden Heart Disease From Routine ECGs, Outperforms Cardiologists
excerpt: Pathway Labs' EchoNext model, validated across 500,000 patients and 20 hospitals, identifies six types of structural heart disease from a standard 12-lead ECG — and led to what researchers call the first AI-detected heart transplant case.
body:
• Pathway Labs' EchoNext AI model has received FDA clearance to detect six types of structural heart disease from a standard 12-lead ECG, including heart failure, valve disease, and pulmonary hypertension.
  • Trained on over 700,000 paired ECGs and echocardiograms from NewYork-Presbyterian, the model outperformed board-certified cardiologists in clinical testing — achieving 77.3% accuracy versus 64% for cardiologists alone.
  • A case published in Nature Medicine documented what researchers describe as the first heart transplant attributable to AI-based disease detection.
  • The company has secured $8.5 million in seed funding and partnered with OpenEvidence to deploy the tool across health systems nationwide.

A Screening Tool for the Most Common Killer

A newly FDA-cleared artificial intelligence tool can now detect multiple types of structural heart disease from a routine electrocardiogram, catching conditions that often go undiagnosed until patients become symptomatic.

The tool, called EchoNext, was developed by Pathway Labs and received clearance for six indications: right- and left-sided heart failure, valve disease, severe hypertrophy consistent with infiltrative cardiomyopathy, and pulmonary hypertension. The underlying research was published in Nature, detailing one of the largest AI-cardiology studies to date.

"While we have mammograms and colonoscopies for cancer, we have never had an equivalent form of early detection for the most common cause of death in the world — heart disease."

— Dr. Pierre Elias, Founder and CEO of Pathway Labs

Elias, who also serves as medical director for artificial intelligence at NewYork-Presbyterian and assistant professor at Columbia University, said the model detects high-risk conditions invisible to the human eye.

Trained on 1.2 Million ECG Pairs

EchoNext was trained on more than 700,000 paired ECGs and echocardiograms collected across the eight-hospital NewYork-Presbyterian system. The full study cohort comprised 1.24 million ECG-echocardiogram pairs from 230,318 unique patients, making it one of the most extensively validated AI-cardiology models available.

In internal testing, the model achieved an AUROC of 85.2% for detecting the composite of structural heart diseases. Performance held across 11 hospitals from four health systems, with no clinically significant variation by patient race, ethnicity, sex, or age.

External validation at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, the Montreal Heart Institute, and the University of California San Francisco showed AUROC scores between 78% and 80% — a modest drop from internal results, but consistent with validation patterns seen across diagnostic technologies.

Beating the Cardiologists

In a head-to-head comparison, 13 board-certified cardiologists reviewed 150 ECGs for signs of structural heart disease. Without AI assistance, their accuracy was 64%. With the EchoNext score visible, accuracy improved to 69.2%. The AI model alone scored 77.3%.

The gap was most pronounced on clinically normal ECGs, where cardiologists achieved 69% accuracy while EchoNext maintained 77% — suggesting the tool is especially valuable for identifying disease hidden behind unremarkable readings.

First Prospective Trial, First AI-Detected Transplant

The DISCOVERY trial, a 100-patient prospective study, confirmed EchoNext's ability to detect undiagnosed cardiac disease in real-world settings. Among high-risk patients identified by the model, 73% were found to have structural heart disease on follow-up echocardiography. In the lowest-risk group, just 6% had disease.

Pathway Labs also pointed to a case published in Nature Medicine in which EchoNext flagged previously undiagnosed heart failure — ultimately leading to what the company described as the first heart transplant attributable to AI-based detection.

Deployment and Funding

Alongside the FDA clearance, Pathway Labs announced a partnership with OpenEvidence, a clinical decision platform the company said is used regularly by more than half of U.S. clinicians. The integration places EchoNext's screening output directly inside an existing workflow, eliminating the need for a separate system.

"FDA-approved AI shouldn't sit siloed in the ivory tower while patients wait years for it to reach them."

— Dr. Travis Zack, Chief Medical Officer, OpenEvidence

The company also announced an $8.5 million seed round led by AlleyCorp and Breyer Capital, with funds earmarked for health system deployment and clinical team expansion.

What This Means for Cardiac Screening

EchoNext joins a growing field of AI tools designed to extract diagnostic signals from the ECG — a test that is inexpensive, noninvasive, and already part of routine care for millions of patients. Medicare has established reimbursement codes specifically for AI-powered ECG analysis, a step that could accelerate adoption.

The broader shift is significant: rather than relying on echocardiography after symptoms appear, AI models can mine existing ECG data for patterns associated with structural disease. For primary care and community settings where echocardiography may not be readily available, tools like EchoNext could meaningfully expand access to early detection.

The research team also released a de-identified dataset of 100,000 ECGs with paired echocardiographic labels, along with model weights and preprocessing code, to serve as a public benchmark for future AI-cardiology research.
nri_angle: AI-powered cardiac screening could expand early heart disease detection in community health settings, including those serving South Asian populations who face elevated cardiovascular risk.
